name: Zoe Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, I'm 27, and I work at Fenwick Tax, a small firm that mostly does returns for freelancers: illustrators, sound engineers, a couple of tattoo artists. I share a house with two friends near the station, and my room costs more than half my pay. Savings-wise, I've got about £400, which is less than a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day is chasing freelancers for their income records, sorting expenses, and drafting their self-assessment returns, which is the yearly tax form. I use AI tools every day to sort bank exports into categories and to draft the polite-but-firm emails about missing invoices. I love that my clients are creative people who are terrified of tax, and I get to make it less scary. What wears me out is that I'm still slow on the technical rules, and Ruth, who owns the firm, has to fix my mistakes on anything unusual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I use these tools all day and I know how often they're confidently wrong. At work I'd say we should keep the bits that help and stop paying for the hype. Online I'd post something about how the real problem for freelancers is still late payment, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the tools I'm good at don't give me much of an edge. I was kind of betting on being the AI person at Fenwick to make up for being weak on technical rules. In a plateau I'm just a junior on low pay in a town with hardly any other firms, and my rent still goes up every March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double down on the technical side, especially property income and VAT, so Ruth stops fixing my unusual cases. I'd keep using the tools for the boring sorting so I can take more clients. And I'd start a little side thing doing bookkeeping for two artist friends on weekends, maybe £150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The AI isn't the problem in AI Plateau, my bank balance is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side bookkeeping actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two friends, Kemi and Jonas, who sell prints and run workshops, have asked me twice already. I'd spend a Sunday afternoon a month each on their spreadsheets with a tool doing the categorising. I'd need to check with Ruth it doesn't clash with firm clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill hurts most right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent rise in March. Last year it went up £45 a month and my pay went up £30. That gap is where my savings go to die.

say: I'd say these tools are often **confidently wrong**.
For freelancers the real problem is still **late payment**, not robots.
think: My **AI skills** stop being much of an edge in a plateau.
I'm still a junior on **low pay** facing a **rent rise** every March.
do: Study **property income and VAT** so Ruth fixes fewer of my cases.
Use the tools for sorting to **take more clients**.
Start weekend **bookkeeping** for two artist friends, about £150 a month.
feel: **Uneasy**; my **bank balance** worries me more than AI.
S0.quote: The AI isn't the problem in AI Plateau, my bank balance is.
fieldNote: She'd **bet on AI skills** to cover a weak technical base; the plateau removes that edge.
Pressure is **rent outpacing pay**, independent of technology.
Moves quickly to a **side income** rather than cutting back.

steps.text: Study property income and VAT rules on two evenings a week
Use AI sorting on bank exports to take on more freelancer clients
Do monthly bookkeeping for two artist friends for about £150

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to squeeze juniors and the freelancers we serve, so the gains need sharing. At work I'd pitch Ruth on using the tools to cut our fees for low-income freelancers rather than just cut staff. Online I'd argue for a law that firms have to retrain people before cutting them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my firm, Fenwick, needs fewer people like the old me and maybe one person like the new me. Sorting, drafting, chasing, checking, that's all on the card. If I'm the one who sets up and checks the tools, I might be fine, but if Ruth decides she can do it all herself with software, I'm gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Ruth in the first month with a written plan: I run the AI setup, we take on forty more clients, and she keeps me. I'd do a short course on tax software automation, the kind that connects bank feeds to returns. And I'd keep the side bookkeeping growing, because I don't want one boss to be my whole income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a buzzy way. I feel like I can see the door, I just don't know if it'll be open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth could do it all herself. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth is 54 and she's quick, but she hates software admin. She once spent a whole afternoon swearing at a printer driver. I think she'd want someone to handle the tools, but she might choose a contractor over a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Callum, who's a junior at the bigger firm across town and doesn't touch AI at all. His whole job is data entry for building firms. I'd be trying to drag him onto a course with me.

say: The gains need **sharing**, because juniors and freelancers get squeezed.
Firms should have to **retrain before cutting** staff.
think: Fenwick needs **fewer juniors**, maybe one who runs the tools.
If Ruth chooses software over a **salary**, I'm gone.
do: Pitch Ruth a **written plan**: I run AI, we take forty more clients.
Take a short course on **tax software automation**.
Grow the **side bookkeeping** so one boss isn't my whole income.
feel: **Anxious** but buzzy; I can see the **door** but not if it's open.
S1.quote: My firm, Fenwick, needs fewer people like the old me and maybe one person like the new me.
fieldNote: She'd **pitch her own role** to the owner rather than wait to be told.
Her risk is real: the owner may prefer a **cheap contractor** to a junior's salary.
Wants **progressive rules** on retraining but plans as an individual anyway.

steps.text: Give the owner a written plan to run the firm's AI setup
Take a short course on linking bank feeds to tax returns
Grow weekend bookkeeping to four artist clients
Campaign online for a retrain-before-cutting rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built this owe the rest of us a living, literally, so tax them and fund a basic income. At work I'd tell Ruth we should be honest with clients about what's coming. Online I'd be loud, I won't pretend I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is pure thinking work, so it goes on day one in 2028. Being good with AI tools doesn't help when the AI doesn't need a person to run it. The three-year gap before robots doesn't save me unless I move into something hands-on, and I'm not a hands-on person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd squeeze every pound into savings, take on as many side clients as I can before 2028, and try to get three months saved. I'd look hard at jobs where a person has to be in the room, like money advice at a community centre or helping artists apply for grants face to face. Once it arrived, I'd join whatever union or tenant group is organising, because my rent would be the first thing I couldn't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing the maths on how many months £400 lasts, and the answer is less than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a hands-on person. Would you try anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's a decorator and he's always said I could help him. I'd hate it, my arms are like spaghetti. But for three years of wages before the robots, I'd probably paint ceilings with him on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your clients, the freelancers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a lot of them are already losing work to image and music tools. So we'd all be going down together. I can't charge them more when their own income's disappearing.

say: **Tax the builders** of AI and fund a basic **income**.
I'd tell Ruth we should be **honest with clients**.
think: My job is **pure thinking work**, so it goes in 2028.
AI skills don't help when the AI doesn't **need a person**.
do: Pile side income into savings aiming for **three months saved**.
Look for **in-person** money advice or grant support roles.
Join a **union or tenant group** once rent becomes the risk.
S2.quote: Being good with AI tools doesn't help when the AI doesn't need a person to run it.
fieldNote: She sees her **AI fluency** as no protection against full AGI.
Would paint ceilings with her **decorator father** to use the robot gap.
Her freelance clients are **falling too**, so the firm loses income from both sides.

steps.text: Take on extra side bookkeeping clients and bank it all
Paint and decorate with her father on weekends
Apply for face-to-face money advice roles at the community centre
Join the local tenants' group as rent becomes unaffordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get a basic income and retraining in place if we start now. At work I'd suggest we build up the advice side so we're not just form-fillers. Online I'd join a group pushing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough to change my whole career once, but not twice. I'd be 32, and I could spend three years moving into something human-facing and still have a couple of years of buffer. The robots coming around 2034 matters less for me, since I'm not going hands-on unless I'm desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd train as a money adviser, the kind who helps people with debts and benefits, through a funded course in the evenings. I'd keep at Fenwick for the pay and keep using AI there to do my work in fewer hours. By year three I'd want to move into an advice charity or a community role, even for a bit less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but planning. Five years feels like a hill, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A bit less money, when you've got £400 saved. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, which is why I'd keep the side clients going. If I've got £300 a month from bookkeeping, I can take a lower salary at a charity. It's tight, but it's a trade I'd make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change anything about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might move to the city, where there are more advice charities and more jobs generally. My housemates would hate it. But this town has three accounting firms and one advice centre, and I'd need more than that.

Firms should build the **advice side**, not just fill forms.

The robot gap matters less, since I'm **not going hands-on**.

Use AI at Fenwick to do my work in **fewer hours**.
Move to an **advice charity** by year three, maybe in the city.
feel: **Anxious** but planning; it's a hill, not a **cliff**.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a hill, not a cliff.
fieldNote: She plans a **single clean pivot** into money advice.
Would use side income to **afford a pay cut**, a deliberate trade-off.
Sees a **move to the city** as likely, given one advice centre in town.

steps.text: Enrol on a funded evening money adviser course next autumn
Use AI at Fenwick to finish client returns in fewer hours
Move to the city by year three for advice charity jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a choice. At work I'd say let's turn Fenwick into the place freelancers come to for money advice, not just tax forms. Online I'd be the annoying optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, or at least I'd have every chance. I'd be 37 with a decade of using these tools, and I could build a little practice of my own advising creative people, with AI doing the paperwork. My accounting tasks still go in 2036, but the trust part with clients can grow for ten years first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish my technical exams so I'm properly qualified. Then I'd build my side clients into a small practice, maybe twenty freelancers by 2030. I'd also join the progressive accountants' network that lobbies for fair tax on tech firms, because I'd want the transition funded properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of hope mixed in. It feels like something I could actually steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you building that practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. You need insurance and software subscriptions, maybe £2,000 to start properly, and I've got £400. I'd have to save it from side clients over a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything personal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay in this town longer, close to my mum and dad. I'd only move if the practice needed it. And I'd stop feeling like I need to decide my whole life by next Tuesday.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and wasting it would be a choice.
Fenwick could become a **money advice** place for freelancers.
think: With a decade I'd **probably be fine** and have every chance.
The **trust part** with clients can grow for ten years first.
do: Finish **technical exams** to become fully qualified.
Build side clients into a **small practice** of twenty by 2030.
Join an accountants' network lobbying for **fair tax** on tech firms.
feel: **Uneasy** with lots of **hope**; it's something I can steer.
S4.quote: I'd stop feeling like I need to decide my whole life by next Tuesday.
fieldNote: With a decade she shifts to **building her own** small practice.
Startup cost of about **£2,000** is her main barrier, given £400 saved.
Ten years lets her **stay near family** instead of moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because being quick with tools is worth nothing if there's no time to turn it into something else. What would help is a basic income or at least a guaranteed wage while retraining, paid for by the companies making the money. Rent controls would help too, honestly, because that's my biggest bill whatever happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my clients' side. Half my freelancers are already watching AI eat their work, and they come to me scared about tax bills on money they no longer have. Every scenario you read me is already happening to somebody I do a tax return for.

headlineQuote: Every scenario you read me is already happening to somebody I do a tax return for.
portrait: Zoe is a 27-year-old **junior** at a small firm doing **freelancers'** tax returns.
She shares a house, has about **£400 saved**, and uses AI tools every day.
Progressive and adaptive, she'd **pitch her role**, grow side clients and push for **tax** on tech.
She's uneasy in the plateau and with ten years, but **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because tool skills are worthless without **time** to pivot.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid retraining funded by AI companies.
**Rent controls**, since rent is her biggest bill in every scenario.
